title: Format Specifiers and Formatted Input and Output
learningObjectives: Match common printf conversion specifications to the promoted argument types they expect.
Explain why scanf usually receives addresses of destination objects.
Check formatted-input return values before using converted data.
Use field width and appropriate length modifiers where required.
Avoid format-string mismatches and validate text received from users.

understand.concept: Formatted input/output functions convert between text and C values according to a format string. printf-family functions receive values, with default argument promotions applying to variadic arguments. scanf-family functions generally receive pointers to destination objects. Each conversion specification has precise requirements; a mismatch can cause undefined behavior. Return values report how many conversions succeeded or whether output failed.
understand.whyItMatters: Input and output are where program data crosses a textual boundary. Correct format strings, return-value checks and input validation prevent corrupted values and misleading output.
understand.analogy: Think of a type as a contract that describes what kind of value an object can hold and which operations make sense for it.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is only an introduction; C types also determine representation, conversions, alignment and constraints.

explain.narrative:
## 1. Formatted output with printf

Include `<stdio.h>` to use printf. Common conversions include `%d` for int, `%u` for unsigned int, `%ld` for long, `%zu` for size_t, `%f` for a double argument, `%c` for a character value and `%s` for a null-terminated character array.

## 2. Formatted input with scanf

For most conversions, scanf expects a pointer to the destination object. Use `&age` when age is an int. For a character array, the array expression supplies a pointer to its first element; set a field width so input cannot overrun the array. Check the return value before using the destination values.

## 3. Length modifiers matter

The format string must match the actual argument type. For example, `%ld` is for long and `%zu` is for size_t in printf. Do not assume a format that works for int is valid for every integer type.

## 4. Validate input

A successful conversion only means the requested conversion was performed. It does not prove the value is within the application's allowed range. Validate ranges and handle trailing or malformed input according to the program's requirements.

## 5. Keep format strings trusted

Use a fixed format string such as `printf("%s", message)` for user-controlled text. Do not pass untrusted text directly as the format string. Format-string mismatches and unbounded input fields are serious defects.

examples.title: Core example
examples.code: int count = 7;\nsize_t length = 12;\nprintf("count=%d length=%zu\\n", count, length);
examples.explanation: %d formats an int and %zu formats a size_t. Match each conversion with the exact promoted argument type.

examples.title: A second case
examples.explanation: scanf needs the address of the destination object and returns the number of successfully assigned input items. Production input handling should also consider trailing characters and line boundaries.

practise.guidedTask: Write a small C program that demonstrates the central rules in CL2.3. Compile with warnings enabled, run it with ordinary and boundary values, and explain each result in your own words.
practise.independentTask: Create a second example for CL2.3 using different values and names. Include one likely mistake as a separate experiment, observe the compiler diagnostic or behavior, then correct it. Record the rule that explains the correction.
hints: Start by identifying the exact type of every object and expression.
Check the C language rule before assuming a platform-specific result.
Use compiler warnings as feedback, not as proof of correctness.
Test normal values and important boundaries.
Explain why the result follows from the language rules.

questions.prompt: Which printf conversion is used for a size_t value?
questions.explanation: The z length modifier is used with u for size_t in printf.

options: scanf needs a pointer to the object where it will store the converted integer
The ampersand converts int to text
questions.answer: scanf needs a pointer to the object where it will store the converted integer
questions.explanation: scanf writes the converted value through the supplied pointer.

questions.prompt: What does a scanf return value of 1 indicate for one requested conversion?
options: One input item was successfully converted and assigned
The input line contained exactly one character
The value is within every application-specific range
questions.answer: One input item was successfully converted and assigned
questions.explanation: The return value counts successful assignments; range validation may still be needed.

questions.prompt: Which call safely prints a user-provided string as data?
questions.explanation: A fixed format string prevents percent sequences in message from being interpreted as directives.

questions.prompt: Why should a scanf string conversion have a field width?
options: To limit how many characters are stored and protect the destination array
To force all strings to be empty
questions.answer: To limit how many characters are stored and protect the destination array
questions.explanation: The width must leave room for the terminating null character.
